chunks: Abu Nasr Hibatullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Katib, the son of the daughter of Abu Ja'far al-Amari (may Allah have mercy on him), narrated, and Abu Nasr said:

He was from the Asadi tribe, but was referred to by his grandfather's name, so he was called al-Amari. A group of the Shi'a have said that Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'Two kunyas, Abu Amr and Abu Ja'far, should not be combined for one person,' and he ordered his agnomen to be changed, so he began to be called al-Amari. He is also called al-Askari, because he was from the garrison (Askar) of Samarra. He is also called al-Samman (the oil dealer), because he traded in ghee (samn) to conceal his status.

key_terms.السَّمَّانُ: Al-Samman (the oil dealer, referring to his trade in ghee)
key_terms.الْأَمْرُ: Al-Amr (the matter of Imamate/authority, often used in Shia context to refer to the Imam's status)
key_terms.الْعَسْكَرِيُّ: Al-Askari (referring to his residence in the military garrison of Samarra)
key_terms.الْعُمَرِيُّ: Al-Amari (a nisba referring to his grandfather Amr or Ja'far Amr)
key_terms.سَرْمَنَ الرَّاؤُ: Samarra (the city in Iraq where the Imams resided during the Minor Occultation)

ai.seo_question: Why was Imam al-Askari known by multiple names like al-Amari, al-Askari, and al-Samman?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* elucidates the multifaceted identity of Imam al-Hasan al-Askari (a.s.), linking his title 'al-Amiri' to his grandfather Abu Ja'far al-Amiri and 'Asadi' and 'al-Samman' to his trade in ghee as a strategic concealment (*kitman*) of his Imamate during the Great Occultation. The text underscores the scholarly tradition of distinguishing between tribal lineage and honorifics, while highlighting the practical wisdom of the Imams in using commerce to mask their political and spiritual status amidst Abbasid surveillance.
